text.p: Following are key facts about Nepal.
POPULATION - About 21 million growing at about 2.5 percent a year (Population Reference Bureau estimate, 1994). Registered voters 12 million (1994 estimate).
Religions - Hindu (89.5 percent), Buddhist (5.3 percent), Moslem (2.6 percent), others, including Christian, (2.6 percent). Nepal is the world's only officially Hindu nation.
Official language - Nepali in the Devanagari script. Hindi and Bihari widely spoken. English used in official and commercial circles. Twelve major dialects are spoken.
Literacy - officially estimated in 1991 at 39.6 percent.

AREA: 141,181 sq km (56,827 sq miles) of plains, Himalayan foothills and the Himalayan range. Mount Everest and seven more of the world's top 10 highest mountains line Nepal's northern border with the Tibetan autonomous region of China. Landlocked Nepal is bordered to the west, south and east by India.
CAPITAL: Kathmandu.

ARMED FORCES: (Source: International Institute for Strategic Studies, 1994-95 survey). Total strength 35,000, plus 28,000 paramilitary police. No tanks, 25 armoured vehicles, some artillery and anti-aircraft guns. No navy. No combat aircraft, four transport planes, eight helicopters. Forces with U.N. missions: Lebanon 598 troops, former Yugoslavia 170 police and observers, Rwanda 2 police observers.

ECONOMY: Nepal, which maintained self-imposed isolation until the middle of this century, is one of the world's 10 poorest countries. Annual income averages $200 a head. Life expectancy 54 years. (Source: World Bank 1996). Infant mortality 95 deaths per 1,000 live births. One physician per 16,000 people. (Health Ministry estimate 1996).
Natural resources are water, timber, hydroelectric potential, scenic beauty, limited but fertile agricultural land, with about 17 percent of its area arable.
Some 59 percent of the population works on farmland that will not support the rapidly growing population. Main products are rice, wheat, jute, millet, maize, sugarcane, oilseed.
Industries include cigarettes, garments, soap, matches, sugar, lumber, jute, cement, wool carpets, gems, leather.

GDP: $4.2 billion in 1996. GDP growth 6.0 percent in 1995/96 (source: Finance Ministry). Nepal's limited development potential lies in water resources and tourism. It produces less than 300 megawatts out of potential 83,000 megawatts. Landlocked, it imports nearly three times the value of its exports with foreign assistance. Geography ties Nepal into the economy of India, where hundreds of thousands of Nepalis work.

Total external debt: $2.1 billion in 1996. Foreign exchange reserves: $775 million, equal to seven months' import requirements. Inflation rate: 9.5 percent in 1996. Foreign aid receipts: $453 million in 1991, or 13.8 percent of GNP (Finance Ministry figures).

Trade deficit in 1995/96 (mid-July 1995 to mid-July 1996) was $1.0 billion (Finance Ministry estimate). Major exports: carpets, garments, hide and skins, pulses, jute, timber. Major export markets: India, Germany, United States. Major imports: textiles, other manufactured goods. Major supplier: India.

MODERN HISTORY: The Shah dynasty extended its rule from its central Gurkha state over other principalities in the late 18th century to form the Hindu Kingdom of Nepal, which remained independent throughout European colonisation of south Asia.
From 1846 the Rana clan took over as hereditary prime ministers, closing Nepal to foreigners until the monarchy, backed by commoners, reasserted its power in 1951.

The late King Mahendra allowed multi-party elections in February and March 1959. The liberal Nepali Congress party won a landslide victory but its leaders were jailed in a palace coup in December 1960. Later King Mahendra banned political parties in favour of non-party councils, or panchayats.

His son succeeded him as King Birendra in 1972. After street protests in 1979, he reformed the panchayat system and held elections for a national, partyless assembly subject to the crown in 1981 and 1986.

Early in 1990 the Nepali Congress and communist factions rallied in mass protests. On April 6, security forces shot dead at least 50 people to stop tens of thousands of pro-democracy demonstrators from marching on the royal palace in Kathmandu.
King Birendra agreed to scrap the panchayat system and let the Nepali Congress form an interim government with communists.

On November 9, 1990, the king made himself a British-style constitutional monarch. The constitution retains Nepal's Hindu status and many Nepalis still revere the king as an incarnation of the Hindu diety Vishnu.

The Nepali Congress won a majority in the new 205-seat parliament in a general election on May 12, 1991. Two rival monarchist parties, both called the National Democratic Party, were routed. The Unified Marxist-Leninist party and its potential leftist allies won two-fifths of the seats to form a formidable opposition.
Girija Prasad Koirala, general-secretary of the Nepali Congress, became Nepal's second elected prime minister on May 26, 1991.
In July 1994, Koirala ordered elections for November after 36 Congress members abstained from a key parliamentary vote.
In November 1994, UML leader Man Mohan Adhikary became Nepal's first communist leader after inconclusive general elections.
In June 1995, King Birendra dissolved parliament on Prime Minister Adhikary's advice and called fresh general elections for November.

But in August 1995, the Supreme Court reversed the decision to dissolve parliament. Sher Bahadur Deuba, 49, of the centrist Nepali Congress party was appointed prime minister and quickly won a vote of confidence.
Deuba, who headed a three-party coalition government with a wafer-thin majority, survived votes of no-confidence in March 1996 and again in December 1996.
But on March 6, Deuba lost a confidence vote which he had called and quickly resigned.

On March 10, a faction of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party led by Lokendra Bahadur Chand, who was twice prime minister under the panchayat system, staked a claim to rule in alliance with the communist UML and two small parties.

King Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev was born on December 28, 1945. His consort is Queen Aishwarya, born on November 7, 1949. They have three children, Crown Prince Dipendra, born on June 27, 1971, Princess Sruti and Prince Niranjan.

Nepal accepts foreign aid from all quarters. It belongs to the United Nations, is one of the Non-Aligned Movement's most genuinely non-aligned countries and an enthusiastic member of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), which is based in Kathmandu.
